payload.question: Should we raise cold brew prices again?

record.line: [no] I would not raise it again. At $5 guests already say it is not worth it and sales fell, so quality and trust are not backing a higher board price.
[strong no] I say no to another rise. Neighbours already hear $5 as too much and cold brew sales fell, so raising hurts footfall and word of mouth. Test dropping back to $4.
[strong no] I see regulars already calling $5 too much and sales dropping, so another raise will push them away for good.
[strong no] I won't raise it again. Volume fell from about 35 to about 20 a day after $5, so another hike kills throughput and margin per shift.
[strong no] I say no raise. At $5 volume fell from ~35 to ~21 a day, so cold brew cash fell from ~$140 to ~$105 daily. Raising more risks more loss; dropping to $4 likely restores cash.
to finance: Finance, dropping to $4 won't fix a lukewarm, inconsistent cup. Hold $5, fix quality first, then the price earns trust.
to chef: Chef, keeping $5 keeps the complaint alive. Neighbours already say $5 is too much, so test $4 and let regulars bring friends back.
to marketer: Marketer, dropping to $4 won't win back regulars who already left over broken espresso; price isn't their breaking point alone.
to finance: Finance, revenue isn't margin. At $5 we sell ~20, at $4 ~35, but without cost per cup, waste and staffing, you can't claim $4 restores profit.
to ops: Ops, keeping $5 protects price but cash is down: volume fell from 37 to 18, so $5 x 18 is less than $4 x 37.
votes amend: Test $4 only after we fix the cup; price cut alone won't earn trust.
votes endorse: Neighbours already hear $5 as too much. Test $4 timed, track footfall, let regulars bring friends back.
votes amend: Regulars already call $5 too much; a timed $4 test shows fairness and gives them a reason to return.
votes endorse: Timed $4 test is right, but only if we track cost per cup, waste and staffing before calling it profit.
votes endorse: Endorse timed $4 test. $5 cut daily cold brew cash, another rise risks more. Track cost per cup before permanent cut.

parsed.label: DON'T
parsed.call: Do not raise cold brew again. Lower to $4 as a one-week test; $5 already cut volume from about 35 to about 20 daily and triggered repeated too-much complaints.

why.point: At $5 volume fell from ~35 to ~21 a day, so cold brew cash fell from ~$140 to ~$105 daily.
Neighbours already hear $5 as too much and cold brew sales fell, so raising hurts footfall and word of mouth.
Volume fell from about 35 to about 20 a day after $5, so another hike kills throughput and margin per shift.

minority.quote: Hold $5, fix quality first, then the price earns trust.
minority.would_have_to_be_true: Quality fix alone restores $5 volume without lowering price.

next_steps.action: Stop any further cold brew price increase; confirm $4 test start.
Run $4 for one week, track daily cold brew volume and revenue.
Review test volume, complaints, and cost per cup before deciding.

parsed.kill_criteria: If $4 week does not lift volume above ~25 daily, revert and reassess.

fights.crux: Price versus quality as cause of lost sales
fights.story: Chef says fix cup first; others say $5 complaints and volume drop show price is the barrier.

conditions: Track cost per cup, waste and staffing before claiming profit
Monitor reviews for cold brew price complaints during test
parsed.cheapest_test: One week at $4, compare daily cold brew units to $5 baseline.
